summary: Perimeter problem-solving for ages 8–9 extends 'perimeter = sum of all sides' in two directions: working backwards to find an unknown side (total minus the known sides), and separating perimeter from area (rectangles with the same perimeter can have very different areas). It rests on labelling every side before adding and keeping units explicit (cm for perimeter, cm² for area).
misconceptions: Adds only the two given adjacent sides of a rectangle, forgetting the opposite pair
Confuses perimeter with area — multiplies the sides or counts interior squares when asked for perimeter
Believes a fixed perimeter forces a fixed area (can't produce two same-perimeter rectangles with different areas)
Drops the unit or mixes cm and m within a problem

activities.title: Watch the area change while the perimeter stays the same
steps: On a 1 cm square grid, draw or take a rectangle (e.g. one with perimeter 24 cm, starting as 5 cm × 7 cm) and record its perimeter and its area in a table with columns for length, width, perimeter and area.
Reshape it to become long and thin while keeping the same perimeter of 24 cm — e.g. go from 5×7 to 1×11 — and record the new area in a fresh row each time.
Compare the rows: notice the perimeter stays at 24 cm while the area changes (e.g. from 35 cm² down to 11 cm²).
Answer: if I only tell you a rectangle's perimeter is 24 cm, can you tell me its area for certain? Explain why not.
activities.insight: A fixed perimeter does not fix the area: rectangles with the same perimeter can have very different areas (although the perimeter still limits how big the area can get, e.g. no 24 cm rectangle has an area above 36 cm²).

activities.title: Label every side, then add
steps: Take a rectangle marked only 8 cm along the top and 5 cm down one side.
Before adding anything, label the two unmarked sides — each equals its opposite side (so 8 cm and 5 cm).
Add all four sides: 8 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 26 cm, and write the answer with its unit (cm).
Repeat for a polygon where only some sides are printed: fill in every side length you can determine, then add them all.
activities.insight: Perimeter is the sum of ALL sides; marking every side first prevents the common error of adding only the two given numbers.

activities.title: Find the missing side by reversing
steps: Take a shape with a known total perimeter but one side blank — e.g. a pentagon with perimeter 30 cm and four sides of 5 cm, 6 cm, 7 cm and 4 cm.
Subtract from the total to find the missing side: 30 − 22 = 8 cm.
Use a total-minus-parts bar or number line to narrate: 'All sides must total 30 cm; I already have 22 cm; so the last piece is 8 cm.'
Explain in your own words why you subtract rather than add here.
activities.insight: An unknown side is the perimeter total minus the sum of the known sides — a total-minus-parts (bar-model) reversal of finding the perimeter.

activities.title: Draw and justify same-perimeter, different-area pairs
steps: On grid paper, draw TWO genuinely different rectangles that both have a perimeter of 24 cm (e.g. 1×11 and 5×7).
Work out the area of each (11 cm² and 35 cm²) and record perimeter in cm and area in cm².
Check your evidence: count the unit lengths around each rectangle to confirm both really measure 24 cm.
State in words: equal perimeter does not force equal area.
Extend (reverse case): try to find two rectangles with the same AREA but different perimeters, and show one pair.
activities.insight: A child who truly grasps the dissociation can construct two different rectangles of equal perimeter with unequal areas — and vice versa — and justify it, rather than just stating a rule.

checkQuestion: Set three tasks and watch how the child works, not just their answers. (1) 'Find the perimeter of this rectangle — it's labelled 8 cm along the top and 5 cm down the side.' (2) 'This pentagon has a perimeter of 30 cm. Four of its sides are 5 cm, 6 cm, 7 cm and 4 cm. Find the length of the missing side.' (3) 'On this grid, draw TWO different rectangles that both have a perimeter of 24 cm, and tell me the area of each.'
checkAnswer: (1) Uses all four sides: 8+5+8+5 = 26 cm (labels the unmarked sides). (2) Sums the known sides to 22 cm and subtracts from 30 → missing side = 8 cm. (3) Draws two genuinely different rectangles both totalling 24 cm perimeter (e.g. 1×11 and 5×7) and gives their different areas (11 cm² and 35 cm²), keeping cm for perimeter and cm² for area, and can say that equal perimeter does not force equal area.
